question: How does oxygen redox contribute to the capacity of battery cathodes?
answer: Oxygen (anionic) redox adds usable capacity beyond what transition-metal redox alone can supply: in alkali-rich oxides, oxide anions (O²⁻) donate electrons during charging—acting as reducing agents—and can be summarized as the formation of peroxo-type species, O²⁻ ↔ (O₂)ⁿ⁻, or as electron holes on oxygen. This excess capacity arises because in Li-/Na-excess (or under-coordinated) environments some O ions are coordinated by fewer than three TM ions, leaving "orphaned"/non-bonding O 2p states lifted close to the Fermi level so they become electrochemically labile alongside the TM t₂g states. The review notes that capacities have even exceeded the transition-metal oxidation limit (e.g., ~180 mAh g⁻¹ in Na₂₋ₓRuO₃, with ~0.4 extra electron per formula unit from reversible O redox, plus a voltage rise from 2.2 V to 3.4 V), and that O redox tends to be more dominant in 4d than 3d TM oxides. However, the reduced O ions tend to bond to each other and leave the lattice as O₂ gas, causing permanent capacity fade and a flammability hazard, so mitigation strategies such as surface fluorination are needed to exploit the extra capacity.
